subtopic: CANADIAN CONTRIBUTIONS TO SPECIAL FUND AND TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN CONTRIBUTIONS TO SPECIAL FUND AND TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that when the pledging conference is convened today at United Nations headquarters in New York to enable countries to pledge voluntary contributions to the United Nations special fund and to the United Nations expanded program for technical assistance, Canada will be pledging a substantial increase in its contribution to the special fund.
The government has authorized that we may pledge $5 million for 1964, and this increase over last year's contribution to the fund of $2.35 million in United States funds is evidence of Canada's support for the important pre-investment technical assistance activities of the special fund and for its able and dedicated managing director, Mr. Paul Hoffman. The special fund has attained only 70 per cent of its target of $100 million.
The target of $50 million for the expanded program of technical assistance was reached in 1963, and Canada's pledge to the expanded program for 1964 is being made at the same level as last year.

subsubtopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the adjournment of the debate last night I was bringing to your attention the fact that during the course of the debate we had three of the main speakers on the government side dealing with the matter before us, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), the hopeful minister No. 2 and the parliamentary secretary. I regret very much that although we were delving at that time into a question of the gravest importance to agriculture, we are speaking to the house this afternoon with both the Minister of Agriculture and the minister No. 2 absent from the house, so perhaps we will have to direct our remarks to the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Beer).
We were very distressed indeed, Mr. Speaker, to hear these three speakers from the government side of the house each in turn devoting the major portion of his speech to partisan politics. This can do no less than inject politics into a debate of the type we are now having, and that is unfortunate for this reason. The hon. member for Peel, in his haste to make a point which was a partisan one, committed a serious error, one
3582	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking which I am sure is going to cause him some embarrassment. In criticizing the former minister of agriculture who had preceded him in the debate he took issue with a statement to the effect that an investment of $15 in fertilizer in the eastern provinces would in fact bring back a return of $100 if the fertilizer were applied to pasture lands used as fodder. This return would be brought back to the farmers in the sale of livestock. The hon. member for Peel said, in effect, that the former minister should check with somebody experienced in producing cattle, because these figures were outrageous.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it embarrasses me no end to bring to task the hon. member for Peel, who was a classmate of mine at university, because one of the things he was taught there was that you should never make a statement like that unless you have the facts to back you up. The former minister of agriculture was not drawing these facts out of a hat; he was quoting from the results of experiments conducted by the Department of Agriculture in Nova Scotia. These are the facts which the hon. member for Peel called outrageous. I submit, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext: I think Hansard will show clearly enough that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said that an application of $15 worth of fertilizer would return $90 to $100 an acre to the farmer in the form of beef. That is not true.

subsubtopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is just my point. This is the point brought out by the Department of Agriculture. If the hon. member would care to peruse the report he will see for himself that that is exactly the statement which was made. If the hon. member for Peel would spend some time at these various experimental stations and farms I think he would be able to learn the facts as they are in this stricken area of the maritimes.
We also heard from the hon. member for Red Deer, and I must pay tribute to him for remembering in his speech Thanksgiving day. I must say also that he expressed some knowledge of the sorry plight of some of the farmers in eastern Canada. But I must take exception to the rest of his speech, because in my opinion it dealt strictly with partisan politics. He tried to vindicate his stand. Although he criticized the policies of the former government he said that he is going to support to a degree the present government; then he turns round and brings in a subamendment condemning this very

practice and indicates to the house that he will, as usual, support the government in any vote against them.
He also made the flat statement, on which I should like to take issue with him, that the former government contributed nothing to the agricultural policies of this country. Mr. Speaker, the name "Hamilton" is a household word on every farm in Canada because of the farm policies initiated by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the government he represented. In fact if the name "Hays" is ever known throughout Canada to the same degree I will be one of the first to laud his efforts on behalf of the farmers of Canada.
I am not going to labour the question as to what the government has or has not done. I think the hon. member for Timiskaming was very fair in his statement that the former government contributed something to agriculture but had made some mistakes as well. That is, as I say, a fair statement. He also stated that this present government may also contribute something to agriculture, and may make some mistakes as well. That too is a fair statement. But I should like to point out that from 1957 to 1962, according to the actual figures, the former government increased the average farm remuneration by 25 per cent. This is not a complacent attitude. This represents extra money in the pockets of the farmers.
After accomplishing that, the former minister became aware of the fact that this increase in remuneration was not uniform, that there were still many farmers not receiving a fair share of farm income. Thus policies were found to correct the grievous situation which existed at that time. That is why the former minister of agriculture turned to the problems of eastern Canada. That is why he advocated assistance to the feed lot operators of eastern Canada. That is why he advocated credit for farm storage, so that grain could be put into the eastern provinces and made available to those who needed it. That is why he advocated an average base mean price for grain for all farmers in the eastern provinces.
He was determined to move feed grain into the east in competition with United States grain moving by ship. He was determined to give the farmers in eastern Canada an opportunity to compete with other parts of Canada in the sale of their livestock. It was he who suggested there should be some deficiency payment or acreage payment to encourage production of livestock feed. It was he who advocated that fertilizer should be used to a greater extent in Quebec and eastern Ontario

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
as well as in the maritimes. These were all progressive steps intended to help eastern farmers.
We were happy to support these efforts by the former minister because we in Ontario, as in other parts of Canada, have a surplus of feed grain and, in my opinion, if we could deliver this grain to the maritimes and put them on a better competitive footing we would be most happy to do so.
I should like to deal now with the so-called policy, or lack of policy, put forward by the three hon. members who spoke from the government side of the house. I might say we found their speeches disappointing. I am sure they have done a great deal of investigating into this serious problem which faces agriculture. I am sure there are many on the government side of this house who are as anxious as we are to help the farmers.
Unfortunately it is impossible for us and for the farmers in this country generally to get any formal commitment as to policy from those hon. gentlemen who sit opposite. We heard the Minister of Agriculture tell us yesterday that income had increased and that the gross national income had gone up too. But we, as farmers, seem to be in the same position as other people; the rich appear to be getting richer and the poor to be getting poorer.
The minister told us he had a farm in the east and a farm in the west, that he had a farm of his own and that he milked dairy cattle. This is most interesting. He also told us that he had visited 32 countries and talked with various ministers of agriculture in those places. If he went to those places to learn, to observe, to study and to consult with those people, then he is to be commended. But in the light of events since April 8 the farmers across the nation are beginning to wonder whether he was, perhaps, sent to those countries in accordance with a definite government policy to keep him out of the House of Commons and, indeed, to keep him out of the country.
We heard a speech from the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane. He too made a partisan speech, but his was a little different. One received the impression that he was preaching for a call and trying to justify another bureau in this already topheavy department of government. He suggested that there should be a second minister of agriculture and that there should be a division of authority although, he was careful to add, they would all work together.
This is most interesting because in Quebec, Ontario and the four maritime provinces
there are already six departments of agriculture with the federal Department of Agriculture making a seventh. Now the hon. member's solution is to add a further department of agriculture. In passing, it seems to me that if this government was as sincere in its efforts to help farmers in eastern Canada as it professes to be, it could have taken advantage of a grand opportunity to make this clear. Hon. members opposite said they would appoint a minister of agriculture for the east. When they returned to power, with so few members from the west, everyone in Canada would have applauded them, I think, if they had appointed a minister of agriculture for the east at that time to take care of this very situation which they are so worried about today.
I was interested in one of the projects mentioned by the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane. He gave the house a review of studies which are being made in the maritimes, in Quebec and in Ontario, and said the government was looking into ways and means of helping the farmers there. There were many good points among those he outlined, but I had the feeling they were brought up in order to create confidence among the farmers of this nation, to make them feel that the. present government was going all out to help them.
One of the points the hon. member made struck me as being strange indeed. He said they had a committee set up-I cannot recall the exact words, but this was the intent- to look into all matters affecting agriculture in the maritimes. How can this statement inspire confidence among the farmers of the maritimes? In April and in the period before that date, they had all the answers. Now, in October, they are looking into the questions.
It is true that in the policy they enunciated before the election hon. members opposite did put forward many points which in my view had a great deal of merit. In fact I should like to see those proposals discussed in the house by members on all sides so that we might decide whether something of a constructive nature could be done to help those farmers of whom wTe are speaking.
A great many promises and commitments were made. In my own area, for example, we grow a large crop of soybeans. What were we told? Candidates representing the party opposite came into the area and said the farmers were entitled to a floor price of at least $2.40 a bushel for those soybeans. Subsequently they established a policy, though the matter was never debated in the house. What was it? It amounted to $2.16 for soybeans.
3584	HOUSE OF
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
Let me give the house another example. They said the time had come to introduce a policy for sugar beets. They said that immediately after a government had been formed they would look into this question of sugar beets. Here we are, many months later-the hon. member for Red Deer said six months-and not a word has been said about sugar beets. This is why farmers across the nation are losing confidence. They looked forward to the arrival of these men. These were the men who had the answers. They were to be the salvation of the farmers of Canada. What disillusionment, what a disappointment they suffered.
I should like to discuss some of the promises which were made to the eastern farmers, the people about whom hon. members opposite now worry so much. They said there would be an increase in farm loans. I think there is some merit in this idea, but I should hate to see the program "blow the lid off" as the Minister of Agriculture described it. They blew the lid off the budget and the country has suffered ever since. I think there should be a great deal of study and thought given to this subject. They were going to increase the freight subsidy and put more crops under the deficiency payment program. They promised to increase research, to establish a higher floor price for wheat, to extend greater assistance to sugar beet and soybean producers. They were going to help the farmer. But here is the real gem. This was said by their leader, speaking in Port Arthur on March 8 last:
Another immediate change would be "changes in the nature of assistance to agriculture, changes without additional burden on our treasury"-
That says no more money in my language- "changes without additional burden on our treasury"-
-and "our farm assistance program will be more effective than the present assistance being given to farmers, but it will not necessarily add to our total expenditures".
Might I point out that a general would love a condition like this where you can charge and retreat, negotiate an armistice and protect both lines at the same time. The farmers are getting tired of these painless potions and pink pills. They want more than verbiage. They do not want to be buried under countless pages of talk, under countless committees looking for ways and means to help them. The farmers know the problems. They know the ills. They know what should be done.
We have in this country one of the finest departments of agriculture in the world. As a matter of fact it is envied by all the world. This department has made advances in agriculture that have amazed the world. This is


the department that minister No. 2 is going to divide. Sir, when we hear them talk about dividing and adding to committees we begin to think about that terrible bugaboo of patronage. We have had too much experience with patronage. When I hear them say that they must increase the number of men in the department who can speak French, may I say I have no objection to men of French origin or the French tongue being taken on staff in the Department of Agriculture. But I do insist on one thing, that the main criterion for a man to join the Department of Agriculture not be the language he speaks but his ability. I do not care what his second language is if his first language is a knowledge of agriculture in Canada.
At the beginning of the session the Minister of Agriculture started to answer our questions. He was a new man faced with a large portfolio and sitting in the house for the first time, and he did make mistakes. The house laughed at times but members were laughing with him, not at him. It was refreshing indeed to have a man come in the house and not give the same old pat answers that we receive time and time again. But all at once he started to give us pat answers and to ask that any question of a controversial nature be placed on the order paper. He had had a conference with the front bench opposite, and he had got his orders. He had got the message. It was to be politics and not facts.
Yesterday we heard the minister challenge the former minister to a milking contest or to see who could plow the straightest furrow. This is reducing the efforts of the Minister of Agriculture right down to the level of a theatrical performance. It is not like the Minister of Agriculture to indulge in such things. But when you see what is going on, when you see this minister asked to take over the portfolio and he does not know whether he has the sole responsibility or whether he has to share the responsibility with someone tomorrow; when wheat sales and the Canadian wheat board are taken away from his department and put somewhere else; when he cannot stand up and give policy as it should be given, one can understand that because of his frustration, disillusionment and impatience with the whole matter he is going to be like a boy kicking a tin can when he does not get his own way. This is why he made the kind of speech he did yesterday.
After watching the Minister of Agriculture in the house since April I certainly believe he has true ability, but he has got to be given a chance. Let him lead the Department of Agriculture. Let him develop it. Let him bring before the house for the first time a government policy on agriculture, and let us

as the parliament of Canada debate this policy. Let us have a say whether it is good or bad. Let us make suggestions and amendments. Let us all get together to see if we can bring forth a real agricultural policy for Canada. Let us not tie up this man with red tape and partisan politics, as is being done today.
Why was it that the former minister of agriculture could make a name for himself and his government? It was because he was given the responsibility for the Department of Agriculture, and was allowed to discharge it and make decisions.
I think the government should introduce a policy. They owe it to the Canadian people to introduce a policy. They gave a commitment and undertaking to the nation that they would have a government farm policy and would introduce it right here in the House of Commons and in the standing committee on agriculture, if that committee is ever activated. We have been here for months and months and they talk about the problems of agriculture, but they have never activated the committee on agriculture.
Let them bring forward a policy and give us a chance to look at it. Give us a chance to study it. Give us a chance to suggest ways and means by which it might be improved. Then we would be giving the farmers of this country some hope. We would have a program then that would be the envy of the world. We would also be upgrading parliament to the stature to which it is entitled. We hear outside the house that parliament is sick, and sick it is, sir. It is sick because the opposition never have a chance to take any part in suggesting amendments or changes with regard to anything affecting the policies of this nation. We have government by decree, not by parliament.
The same thing applies so far as agriculture is concerned. We want to know what is going on. What does the government intend for agriculture? We have farmers all across the nation with large businesses who are depending on the remuneration from the sale of their crops. We want to know what the plans of the government are to market these crops. We want to know what plans they have for the eastern farmers. We want to know how they are going to activate ARDA. We do not want to be told that there is going to be one committee after another, that this or that matter is being taken into consideration, that due consideration is being given and that when a policy has been formulated it will be announced in the house. This is not good enough.
Surely the time has come that this government should stand on its feet, act like a party, act like Canadians and put before the
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking house a definite Canadian policy on agriculture, so that for the first time we can act like a parliament and represent our constituencies to the degree that we can be proud of the work that we are doing here in Ottawa.

subsubtopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like, first of all, to congratulate heartily the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who, through his amendment to the motion that the house go into committee of supply, gave us the opportunity to discuss agriculture.
I should also like to commend him for the fine statement he made regarding the problems of eastern farmers. He proved that he was aware of all their problems. He suggested some extremely interesting solutions and I wish to congratulate him for the improvement he has shown over the last year. As a matter of fact, if he had been as knowledgeable, as competent and as devoted to eastern farmers when he was minister, I can assure you that we would not be facing the same problems today.
What did he do when he was minister of agriculture in the previous Conservative government? On February 6, 1963, he placed on the order paper of the house a resolution prior to the introduction of a bill affecting the farmers, but he presented it at that time when he was sure the bill would never be passed by the house; it was the day after his government had been brought down.
All he wanted to gain with that bill was political capital. He wanted to have something to talk about during his election campaign. But the Canadian voters saw right through him and they turned out of office and for good the worst government that the country had ever known since the years 1930-35.
Mr. Speaker, Social Crediters were blamed for joining us in bringing the government down on the evening of February 5, 1963. But Social Crediters had had enough of the inefficiency of the government of that time, which had become obvious to all Canadians.
They could no longer explain to their electors the attitude they had taken and followed in this chamber until February 5, 1963. And it is not because they wanted an election. We did not want one either because we had had enough of elections. We had barely come out of an extremely tiring election campaign; but we had an objective, that is the welfare of the Canadian people. We wanted to give to the Canadian people the government they had a right to have, a Liberal government, and

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking that is what ws did. That is why we led the previous government towards a general election.
What did the Conservatives do for the welfare of the agricultural community during the six years they were in office? They put into effect a policy of grants to win the sympathy of the farmers: grants for feed, butter and cheese. Besides, they bought surpluses. They piled up millions of bushels of grain, millions of pounds of butter, so much that, at a certain time, the former minister of agriculture was afraid.
Mr. Speaker, it is said that fear is the beginning of wisdom, but in the case of the former minister of agriculture, that does not apply. What did the then minister of agriculture do when he saw we had millions of pounds of butter and millions of bushels of grain in storage? He said to the western farmers: we can sell our grain to the Chinese, but unfortunately, we have fears concerning payment. We are afraid Canadian people will not be paid for their grain, so I ask you to endorse the Chinese and to insure, as it were, the credit we are extending to them.
His speech was not greeted by applause and he did not speak about it again.
And what did he say to milk producers? He told them: We have butter and cheese surpluses.
To those he had encouraged to increase their herds, to improve their equipment, he said: Sell your cows, we have too much milk.
Again, he was not warmly received.
On February 5, 1963, the former minister left agriculture in the worst stagnation ever known in Canada; but the following day, on February 6, he knew all the answers. During his election campaign, he said that the Liberals had misled farmers.
But, Mr. Speaker, who wants to mislead the Canadian farmer? The one who passes measures, even unpopular ones, believing sincerely that they are bound to solve problems, by getting at their very root, or the one who leads the farmers to bankruptcy while telling them that everything is fine?
Who wants to deceive Canadian farmers? The present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), who sells our dairy surpluses and advocates a policy of such a nature as to direct production according to needs, on the domestic market as well as on the export market, or the former minister of agriculture who, by promoting surplus production, by granting subsidies and support prices was leading agriculture to a dead end?
Who is deceiving farmers? The former minister of agriculture or the present minister who is sincerely devoted to our farmers?
Mr. Speaker, I do not entirely approve of the various things done by our present

minister; beside, I regret that he has not seen fit to do other things, which to me seemed highly desirable.
I am sorry to see that the legislation for appointing a minister of agriculture for the east has not yet been submitted to the house. The eastern farmers are waiting for the adoption of the bill, as they are impatient to make their voice heard inside the cabinet, an opportunity they have not had for a good many years.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot be pleased, either, with the priority prescribed by the Minister of Agriculture. Like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I feel that the top priority problem facing eastern farmers is the supply of feed grain.
Eastern farmers lie at the mercy of a group of speculators who control feed grain and who make millions by a few strokes of the pen. Those people freeze sales to boost prices. They also get a large share of the subsidies which the government has established to help farmers.
Whether a farmer produces milk or crops or whether he is a cattle breeder, he must be able to buy feed grain at a reasonable price.
That is why, in my humble opinion, the distribution of feed grain should be nationalized in eastern Canada and a crown corporation set up to control feed grain shipping, storing and wholesale selling in eastern Canada after firm contracts have been negotiated with the Canadian wheat board.
I quite agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when he says that eastern farmers should have the same advantages as the Chinese, Russians, and Japanese who buy our wheat at a fixed price. However, what did the hon. member do when he was minister of agriculture to provide eastern farmers with the same advantages as the Chinese? What did he do?
The proposed crown corporation should control the shipping of grain and the government should pay the whole cost of the operation. At present, the government pays approximately $18 million in freight assistance for feed grain. If those subsidies were to cover the whole cost of shipping, they would amount to about $40 million a year. I feel that we can afford such an expense, the more so since those subsidies would contribute to the establishment of a uniform wholesale price throughout Canada, so that grain would cost the same in Halifax, Quebec city, lake St. John, Montreal, Three Rivers and Fort William.

The setting up of such a body would be most beneficial. First of all, our eastern farmers could depend on a steady supply 12 months a year. We could eliminate the blocking caused by speculators at the present time for price increases. Prices would go down and this would help to lower the production costs. Our milk products could face world competition. We could sell our butter, our cheese and our milk powder at reasonable prices on world markets without the government having to subsidize the manufacturing costs to the extent of 50, 60 and even 75 per cent.
I think that the savings made by the government in that way, could completely cover transportation costs of grain to the east. It could also pay for the setting up of a crown corporation to look after that government control.
Our farmers would then be able to take the place they are entitled to on the national consumer's market. We would not need those many million fowl and poultry which were imported from the United States when the former minister of agriculture was responsible for the future of our farming industry. Indeed, we may recall that in a single fiscal year, we brought in more than 20 million birds from the United States, while we had in eastern Canada producers who could have supplied the market. But, because they are paying too much for their feed grain, they are unable to meet the competition of American chickens and turkeys which are dumped on our market.
Our farmers could increase their production of livestock. We have, in the east, the best pastures in Canada. We do not suffer from drought like the western farmers.
We have land unsuitable for cultivation which is declared as less than marginal every time a survey is made. Such land would make excellent pasture for livestock.

It appears that the former government wanted, by this legislation under date of February 6, to settle all its problems. However, we never saw the bill. Has the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) ever seen this remarkable bill?

They are business men who are there to make profits. I cannot blame them in any way, but if they could be advantageously replaced by a government agency which would adequately perform the work that may be required of a third party between the Canadian wheat board and eastern farmers, why not?

Mr. Speaker, the greatest difference between agriculture in the west and agriculture in Quebec can be seen in many areas. I could enumerate many of them, but I will touch on only one point before I close my remarks.
At this stage, I might open the eyes of the minister on a problem he has not even thought about. And if the minister will take the trouble to consider the remedies he could bring to agriculture to revive its lost strength, he is just at the beginning to get surprises. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that in the west, when they talk about farming a land, they mean that they have to prepare the soil for the seeding, they mean to roll back the forest to make room for wheat. At home, in Quebec, on our modern farms that is not it at all. That marvellous era of conquerors of the primitive soil has disappeared. Today, in Quebec, to return land to farming means fighting an army of financiers who were able by some feat to chase off our best farmers and leave all those large farms empty and barren, like a forest devastated by fire.
In 40 per cent of our farming areas, a deadly silence prevails because animal life is no longer there and man himself, crushed under debt and expelled by usurious moneylenders tolerated by our Canadian legislation, took refuge in the cities, in the shadow of the financiers' skyscrapers which go up at the same rate as the level of our agriculture goes down.
That, gentlemen, is the real problem in Quebec.
When one thinks there are such moneylenders completely foreign to our province who now own 30, and even 40 lots, of our best farms because an irresponsible government allowed the exploitation of the
[Mr. Gauthier.l

farmer who, not so long ago, was prosperous and the pride of our province but who today joins the line, which is already too long, of those under public assistance in our towns and villages.
Mr. Speaker, you see at once that rehabilitation in Quebec cannot be settled by the Department of Agriculture alone, but by the concerted action of the federal government and the department itself.
Is it possible that, after 300 years or more of existence, and nearly one hundred years after confederation, the federal government has not yet succeeded in determining the interest rate in Canada?
It is unthinkable for the common man, and unexplainable for us legislators in this house, to find that no government, until now, has been able to curb, by determining a limit to the interest paid in our country, the army of thieves which has spread all over Canada.
In all the other fields our legislation is very strict and that is a very good thing in order to maintain law and order.
Even in the case of petty crimes, if the thief is caught, he will be fined or put in jail. That is all right.
But tell us please when will measures be taken against the master thieves? What price did they pay all the former governments to keep quiet and what means do they still use, at the present time, to benefit from complete protection, I was even going to say the blessing, of all governments?
We demand laws. The members of the New Democratic party have presented two bills in this respect. I introduced one myself and it is still at the bottom of some drawer.
When time has come to go to the rescue of our farmers, the bills which would save them stay on the order paper of the house waiting to go and die before the banking and commerce committee, because it seems that those which cross the threshold of a committee room do not leave it any more.
Therefore, to ensure the survival of our farmers, we propose that the house should determine as soon as possible the maximum interest rates a lender may charge, retroactive to ten years ago.

This is the Prime Minister of Canada. He made a speech in Port Hope, Ontario on March 5, 1963. Here is what he said:
The emphasis on price supports will be shifted from butter to skim milk powder-
I went back to my place and told that to the farmers. They said, "He is fooling. He does not know what he is saying". I said, "Why?", because I knew what he had said. They said, "It is impossible to make skim milk powder without making butter." One day I had a discussion with the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Tremblay). We talk the same language. I ask him also whether the present government has reduced the production cost by levying this tax which will soon reach 11 per cent, and which the Canadian farmer will have to pay on cement, and everything he will need to improve his farm buildings as well as his cattle stalls? Is the production cost reduced by the levying of a tax on everything the farmer must use to raise his standard of living, to operate his farm in an economical way?
We must reduce the production cost in the province of Quebec, but the way the present government acts does not permit us to succeed.
Mention has been made yesterday of feed grain. Indeed, the Minister of Agriculture stated that this year, there are in the eastern elevators more grain, more barley, more oats than last year at the same date. Well, can the minister tell us who owns this grain, this barley, these oats that are now in the elevators of eastern Canada?
It is likely that the price of grain will be raised after the closing of navigation, because transportation by ship costs $4.50 per ton while it costs $13 by train.
The hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Drouin) was right in complaining of that attitude of the minister, and
I congratulate him for not accepting that new policy which, in my opinion, is entirely unfair.
Perhaps there is an improvement, but I suggest it is not a desirable one, because speculators are still there. They will probably increase the price of grain by $8 per ton instead of offering a regular price to Canadian farmers.
Japan bought from Canada, and the Japanese authorities know exactly how much the grain will cost them for eight months to come. Why not have the same thing in the east?
The bill of the Conservative government about feed grain was aimed at stabilizing the supply in the eastern section of the country, to establish price equalization, even to favour the production of grain in eastern Canada and finally to assure the stability of prices.
To that effect-and the present Minister of Agriculture is aware of that-a survey was made by the staff of the rural economy division of the Department of Agriculture. That survey concerning the problem of feed grain in the eastern part of the country was intended to give a general idea of some of the problems the government had to solve before making such a legislation operative.
Where are we, today, October 15, 1963? Are there interested people who do not want that legislation put on our statute books? Those are questions that farmers we meet ask themselves, and I also put them to the government.
Mr. Speaker, is the answer to all those questions, as the Minister of Agriculture has already stated, that this legislation will enable the federal government to save $6 to $8 million?
Should that be the case, let us remember that the farmers, particularly in Quebec, where 60 per cent of the farms bring in less than $2,400 per year in gross income, cannot afford to accept that kind of policy.
Our farmers are ready and willing to play their part, that is to say:
1.	Feed the world with quality products, at minimum prices.

However, the farmers are conscious of the fact that they have a third role to play, especially this year, because in our part of the country the crops were poor. This third role is to earn a decent living.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. While we do enjoy a limited amount of this verbal Quebec tid-dledy-winks, we do not want to lose our opportunity to take our places in this debate. I rise to express our support for the subamendment. While I think that most hon. members will agree that the subamendment is clumsily worded, it is without a doubt intended to say that both old line parties have failed to implement policies which would result in a Canada-wide stable and prosperous agricultural economy. However, in the interests of biculturalism I trust that future subamendments introduced by the hon. and learned member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) will indicate a greater respect for the beauty and precision of the English language. I think that anyone reading the subamendment carefully will agree with us that it does require some literary spinal adjustment.
This debate has been infected by the same lack of constructive purpose that has characterized several previous debates this session. For members on the government side of the house and members of the official opposition to continue their pot-calling-the-kettle-black form of debate is to demonstrate a lack of responsibility which will in time undermine confidence in parliament and engender a lack of respect for members of this house. Speaking on behalf of this group I want to reiterate and emphasize the fact that we believe that, under the present circumstances possibly more than ever, it is our responsibility to deal with these matters in a constructive way. The members of this group believe that we should take advantage of this debate to discuss agricultural policies and legislation in relation to changing needs and circumstances, and believe that it is the duty and function of the opposition to advance constructive alternatives to government policies and proposals. That is what the hon. members of this group have tried to do in this debate.
Now, Mr. Speaker, Canadian agricultural policy naturally contains many unusual ramifications and diversifications. It must, in order to meet the needs of farmers from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The size of our country, its geography, varieties of climate, variations in soil and many variations in conditions present problems which can only be met effectively on the basis of members of this house having complete information and the facts with respect to the problems with which they are called upon to deal. These problems can only be met as a result of co-operation
between federal and provincial governments, between governments and farmers' organizations and other groups in the community, and the understanding and active participation of large sections of the rural community by way of giving effect to leadership given by government, and the implementation of the policies announced by government.
I have been appalled, Mr. Speaker, in listening to this debate, at the ignorance of the situation we face today, and at the lack of facts and information upon which to base our decisions on these most important questions. Therefore, I suggest that it is one of the first duties of the members of this house to become informed on all the various questions and problems relating to agriculture, such as land use, production, overseas marketing, transportation, research, farm credit, crop insurance and the relationship between agriculture and the rest of our economy. All this offers a wide field for investigation and study on the part of members of this house. I have done some reading on this question. I have always been interested in agriculture, as have other members of this group. In our own agriculture committee we try to have members undertake studies of certain questions of which they have some knowledge from experience. My hon. friend from Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) was brought up on a farm and has had a lot of experience in farming. My hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) has also demonstrated his knowledge of farming. On one occasion he came to our ranch when I was absent, arriving at a time when there was a certain crisis in the barnyard. I can say, without exaggeration, that he attended to the obstetrical ceremonies required by an ancient cow with dignity, distinction and complete aplomb.
The subject of agriculture and its relationship to government policy generally has, of course, been the subject of considerable study and investigation by persons interested both from a scientific and from a practical point of view. I wish to quote briefly from the November-December, 1960, issue of the Agriculture Institute Review. I think the persons who wrote this article made some excellent observations on the subject of the relationship between agriculture and public policy. The article is entitled "Agricultural Legislation in Relation to Changing Need" and it was written by M. Brownstone and C. Schwartz. They are discussing public policy in its relation to farming, and this is what they have to say:
At the same time, the analysis points towards the central role which the state must play in solving farm problems in accordance with output and income criteria.

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
Despite the validity of this general proposition, significant advances have been made in specific instances where policies have been based solidly on careful and realistic appraisal. Unfortunately, even these advances may well be handicapped by lack of a comprehensive approach-as was pointed out in the case of resource adjustment via farm credit.
One important disability in the effort to build public policy-
They are talking about agricultural policy.
-is divided jurisdiction and its political manifestations. This aspect of our constitution has provided an historic technique for escaping responsibility and for misplacing responsibility. But this is by no means applied consistently. In farm credit, for instance, we have reasonably full expression of national interest and policy combined with ample opportunity for provincial variations. But the development of marketing policy has been replete with skilful evasive tactics leading to an hiatus every decade. And crop insurance is an excellent example of federal power being used very effectively to minimize federal responsibility and potential embarrassment on the one hand and on the other to virtually coerce the provinces into unwilling acceptance of the more onerous and burdensome aspects of such a program.
The farmer as the focus of all this remains largely exposed to the economic elements. Clearly he has not developed an effective political voice any more than he has welded together a solid farm movement. Undoubtedly Canadian farmers could gain strength if (1) they could and would unify in a policy sense; (2) they would approach their problems with greater realism and understanding of the total economy and its dynamics; (3) make greater use of their own economic organizations, largely in the co-operative form; (4) form an alignment with other groups in our economy whose basic aims are not in fundamental conflict with those of the farmer. In this manner, the farmers can perhaps offset their undoubtedly waning political influence as farm population continues to decline both absolutely and relatively. Of course, as against this we have a little prairie homily which goes something like this; "It's not the size of the barking dog that counts but the size of the dog's barking".
I think there are some interesting comments to be found in that article and I would recommend hon. members to look it up in the library.
In this group we try to make constructive proposals with regard to any of the subjects we are called upon to debate in this house. We recognize the complications and difficulties surrounding agricultural legislation and policy. We do not think it is sufficient to refer continually to the past and to say "You did this" or "You did not do that and so on". We had, in the late James Gardiner, despite all the criticisms which were made of him, a particular champion of prairie agriculture and we had in the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) a man who was thoroughly devoted to the cause of agriculture and who was responsible for having some good legislation placed on the statute books, particularly the ARDA measure, and the Farm Credit Act. I think there is credit due to both sides, and
[Mr. Herridge.l
criticism to both sides, as well. However we must look to the future and the solution of these difficulties will require more than just superficial debate. It will require a close study of all the circumstances surrounding the industry in all its aspects from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I suggest that this need offers a great opportunity for the agriculture committee of this house to function as never before in order to provide a basis for sound agricultural policies. It should undertake a study of these aspects of agriculture about which many members of this house and many people in Canada know very little. I suggest that the occasion presents an opportunity for a committee of the other place to co-operate with the agriculture committee of this house. There should be some planning of this work. I give full credit to the committees of the other place which have undertaken studies of such important subjects as the narcotics problem, the manpower question and the question of land use. Some very useful and constructive work has been done by the committees of the other place which have studied these matters, and I think we should secure the co-operation of the other place in sharing the heavy burden which is imposed by the needs of the moment with respect to understanding the facts relating to agriculture. I suggest that some effort be made to plan this study as between the agriculture committee of this house and the appropriate committee of the other place. A committee should be established and it should call before it senior members of the Department of Agriculture. The first thing to know is the workings of the Department of Agriculture. I have met members of the house who have very little knowledge of how the various branches of the Department of Agriculture work and what their functions are. I think we should get the views of the senior officials on the administrative machinery of today. I believe we should have representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and of the farmers' unions come before the committee to give evidence and express their opinions. We should have representatives of the fruit growers' organization, the poultry association, the beekeepers and all other farm organizations and those interested in and related to agriculture.
I think we should also get the views of the farmers' wives through the rural women's organizations, because in order to understand the problem we must have the views of all those serving agriculture and working in agriculture. I think we should ask representatives to appear from the Agricultural Institute of Canada, an organization composed of graduates in agriculture and allied sciences

who are giving considerable study to this question and have throughout the years. I think representatives of the Agricultural Institute of Canada could make a valuable contribution to the information on this very important question.
I also suggest that we should have representatives of the Canadian tree farmers association come before the agriculture committee, and I do so because in Great Britain and in Sweden and other European countries tree farming has always been very closely related to agriculture. I am talking about private tree farming undertaken by farmers and others as a part time occupation. Many aspects of tree farming are under the administration of the agricultural departments in these countries, and their agricultural organizations foster this other aspect of farming.
I suggest that we should call before the committee representatives of the tree farmers of Canada so they can tell their story as to the relationship of private tree farming to the development of the family farm, and give us their advice. I also believe we should call representatives of other groups who wish to give evidence before the committee and who can contribute something to the information and knowledge of the committee. We should also ask representatives of the cooperatives and credit unions to come before the committee and give their views with respect to co-operative marketing, agricultural credit and so on.
I know that this represents a pretty heavy agenda, Mr. Speaker, but in my view this is something that must be undertaken if members of the house are going to pay the close and careful attention to agricultural problems that is demanded of them under present circumstances. I say once again it is not sufficient to charge one another superficially with failing to do this or failing to do that.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the debate on the motion brought forward by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), I wish to emphasize the reasoned, practical approach that he took in presenting his motion to the house. He brought to our attention a problem that deserves the consideration of all hon. members. In outlining the problem he brought forward statistics that portray in dramatic detail the fundamental change that has been taking place in our basic economy, in our basic industry, agriculture. This is a process that began a number of years ago, indeed even before the second world war, but it has accelerated within the past few years."
These changes have taken place for several reasons, because of the necessity of mechanization of our farms, because of advances in technology, because of improved land use practices, because of improved cultivation practices and the use of fertilizers, and certainly because of the tremendous competition there is in agriculture and the need to make our agriculture plant as efficient as possible. I do not think there is a group in the Canadian economy that has proceeded at the pace agriculture has in increasing efficiency of production.
But with this growth and with these adjustments have come problems. Contrary to what has been suggested by some hon. members, I do not think there is a panacea. I do not think there is one single solution. I do not think we can deal with these problems by adopting national policies applicable to all parts of Canada in the same manner. The speech of the then prime minister on August 30, 1958, emphasized this point. He emphasized that in reality there were two problems, first of all a national one that had to be dealt with by national policies and then par' allel with the national policies must go regional policies to deal with particular situations that arise from time to time. One year there may be a problem in the maritimes. Another year there may be drought on the
3602	HOUSE OF
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking prairies. Certainly no one can say that national policies can deal with such situations because they are all different, and the methods of farming are different in these areas.
I suggest there are five basic considerations that must be met in the development of an agricultural policy. First of all, it must meet the requirements of the constitution. In other words, does the federal government have authority in that particular field or is it a matter of provincial authority? Is it possible to develop policies that are the joint responsibility of the provincial and federal governments? We have such programs in effect today, and I refer to crop insurance.
Then, will these policies-and we must avoid this at all costs-result in circumscribing the personal freedom of the farmer to make a decision himself? I think this is important, that the power to make decisions remain in the hands of the farmer. Third, are these policies in keeping with the needed adjustments in the farm industry in view of the foreseeable long term trend? Fourth, is the policy flexible enough to permit adjustment and change as the need arises? Fifth, and this is academic but nevertheless important, will it do the job that it is intended to do?
I suggest to you, sir, that if we are to develop policies that are going to meet the needs of this industry it is necessary that these five basic requirements be met. I think every member regarded his speech with some consternation and was somewhat appalled at the attitude the minister took. The statistics presented by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I felt, were undeniable. They were reliable and they pointed out a problem. subsubtopic: COMPANY, COMPETITION WITH PRIVATE ENTERPRISE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance this evening, and to put it in a nutshell for hon. members it has to do with the government allowing civil servants to make policy in the Northwest Territories instead of merely carrying out policy. This means that the government has abandoned its duty to control and give direction to its servants, with the result that the private enterprise sector of the economy has suffered. I am talking, Mr. Speaker, about Northern Transportation Company, which is a crown corporation answering to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) and which is in direct competition with Yellowknife Transportation Company and Arctic Shipping Company. These two private carriers operate along the Mackenzie river and in the Arctic ocean.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that some members may not be very interested in this subject. I would be quite willing to allow a couple of minutes for them to take their private conversations outside because I know that if I speak more than five minutes at this volume my voice will collapse. When the Northern Transportation Company was set up, it had a very simple job to do, namely that of, supplying Eldorado Mining and Refining at Great Bear lake. Originally, the supplying of fuel in the Arctic was taken on by that company, despite the fact that Yellowknife Transportation, a private concern, was already there and ready, willing and able to undertake the supply job. Many years back, under a former Liberal government, we saw the first step taken which put into the Arctic a company to compete with private enterprise and which violated the rule we have that the government should only provide these services where private enterprise is unable to carry out the needed functions.
Mr. C. D. Howe, who was a member of the former Liberal government, talked about the Northern Transportation Company in this house on several occasions. He said it was not the purpose of that company to complete with private enterprise. He made it very clear that he would have been most surprised at the suggestion there was competition between Northern Transportation and other companies, and expressed the view that Northern Transportation was merely carrying out its function of supplying government agencies in those places where private enterprise was unable to do so.
The situation today, Mr. Speaker, is that Northern Transportation and the Yellowknife

company are competing neck and neck throughout the whole length of the Mackenzie river and the Arctic ocean. As recently as this year, Northern Transportation assumed a new role in the Arctic ocean for the first time. They have gone into the business of carrying bulk oil in competition with Arctic Shipping. I submit that there is a very real grievance on the part of those shareholders in Arctic Shipping who see this trend, and who realize that unless this government stops the civil servants from trying to compete with private enterprise, then the private companies will have to fold up.
I have asked some pertinent questions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning government policy. The most significant answer he gave was to the effect that Northern Transportation Company believed in operating in a businesslike way; that it would continue to improve, repair or replace its equipment as needed. This response to my question about competition indicates the businesslike way in which this company has abandoned its previous role of a crown agency supplying services which were not available, and has developed into an agency competing for every bit of business it can get from private enterprise, just as if it was another private company, and just as if it were answerable to shareholders who wanted to make a profit out of their investment.
I submit that the only reason Northern Transportation Company executives are interested in expanding that business is not to provide further service in the Arctic which cannot be provided by private enterprise, it is not for the good of the government, but is merely a little more empire building by some civil servants who like to feel that they can go to the north. I am sure that any hon. member of this house who has ever been in Canada's Arctic will realize that more than half of the total business of the area is government business, and more than half of the people gainfully employed are working for the government. These civil servants want to take advantage of their position. They want to do some empire building to build up their own name, but they forget that their duty is to the public.
The people for whom I speak are not that worried about government competition, if the government competition were subjected to the same rules and the same regulations as private enterprise. The Northern Transportation Company, in addition to having a natural advantage through its government connections, has stacked the deck. Three years ago the Yellowknife Transportation Company tried to get an L.S.M. ship into Canada. They believed this former wartime vessel could
Northern Transportation Company play a very useful role in the transportation of some kinds of goods, and that this ship would enable them to handle their business more efficiently. However, Canadian maritime regulations prohibit the entering into Canada of a vessel more than five years old. This ship was considerably older and the company was refused permission to bring it into the country. The company then built new tugs and new barges at great expense to handle the business as best they could.
The Yellowknife Transportation Company, a private company, was refused permission to bring in the boat, but this spring the Northern Transportation Company, a crown company, brought in the sister ship, another L.S.M., to Vancouver. They started refitting that boat. They knew that the maritime regulations would not permit this, but they sought a government order in council to bypass the maritime commission. I am afraid the minister's answer to me in the house the other day in which he said that the maritime commission would not allow Northern Transportation to further equip the vessel is not quite accurate. It is the vessel itself that comes under maritime regulations. We have the spectacle now of a vessel in Vancouver being re-equipped to do a job in the north, the very thing which our government prohibited private enterprise from doing three years ago. I do not know at the moment how much money the government has wasted on this project. If they are going to make Northern Transportation Company return that vessel, then we have a good grievance against them for wasting this money. Certainly, we have a grievance against the officers of this crown corporation, because not only was private enterprise prevented from doing this same thing three years ago, but the crown corporation, knowing their vessel was three times too old to comply with the maritime regulations, have decided to go ahead and bring it in anyway. They feel that they can get away with what they want.
The answers the minister has given to me in this house and in private conversation, the manner in which the head of the Northern Transportation Company and the deputy minister of Trade and Commerce have acted, indicate that these civil servants either have not told the minister the truth or he is not quite able to understand what they have told him.
It certainly indicates that the Minister of Trade and Commerce fails to understand what is going on in his department. His conversation with me indicates that they do not believe in this extension of competition between the crown and private enterprise, and meanwhile his officials continue on a course

Northern Transportation Company of action which can have no other end result but to knock all private competition out of the north and will within the next year knock out one of the two companies operating up there.
I suggest that hon. members on all sides of the house have the same stake in this matter that I have. The mere fact that the two companies which are suffering at the present time operate in the far north does not make any less serious the fundamental objection that I am sure will be taken by everyone in this house, that we have the crown entering actively into business in competition with private enterprise when there is no need for it; and going even further, taking unfair advantage. I hope some other hon. members who are aware of this problem will go a little further in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my comments to those of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent), particularly in relation to the massive program of extension and building that this crown corporation, Northern Transportation Company, has entered into in direct competition with a private shipping company in the Canadian northwest. In particular I want to point out the failure of Northern Transportation Company to make use of local people from the north on their freighting operations. There is an extensive labour pool of Eskimo and Indian people along the Mackenzie river and along the Arctic coast now being serviced by Northern Transportation Company. The policy of this crown corporation is in direct contrast to policies followed by the private enterprise operation, Yellowknife Transportation, and Arctic Shipping Company, whose policy it was to hire-and still is-Eskimo and Indian people. In fact these private firms have gone so far as to send Indian and Eskimo people from the Northwest Territories to Vancouver at company expense, where they can be taught the skills necessary to qualify them for river operation. As I say, when Northern Transportation Company embarked upon this program of expansion into the Arctic, they did not use the local labour force that was available.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona has already mentioned that Northern Transportation Company expanded after taking over a small operation from the Hudson's Bay Company. Many experts on the north have a great deal to say about the Hudson's Bay Company and its method of operation. But there is one thing no one can take away from the Hudson's Bay Company; they did make extensive use of Eskimo and Indian people in all phases of their operation. This


was particularly true in terms of their shipping operations in the Canadian Arctic. However, when Northern Transportation Company began its expanded operations this summer, the company imported hundreds of workers from southern Canada into such Arctic communities as Tuktoyaktuk, where there was already a labour pool of trained Eskimo people who had no other employment opportunities, now the Hudson's Bay Company was not operating shipping services.
I also want to point out the conflict or the apparent paradox between what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) tells us in this house in relation to private enterprise in the north, and statements made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing). In particular I want to refer to an article printed in the northern newspaper entitled News of the North of September 5. I might point out that the editor of this newspaper is an executive officer of the Liberal party of the Canadian north, so we must assume that everything he says is absolutely correct. He describes the visit of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, when he told Yellowknife people:
Mr. Laing foresaw the gradual withdrawal of the government from economic fields as private industry came into the north.
However, when questioned about this in the house, the minister denied that he had made such a statement. My point is this. I have also a very, shall we say, personal interest in this matter because the towns of Fort McMurray and Waterways, which have pioneered the north, rely on the Northern Transportation Company to a great extent for employment. With the cutback in the production of uranium at Uranium City these two towns have been seriously hit. It is only fair to say that this crown corporation has been looking for other contracts in order to keep the payroll adequate to support these two towns. My suggestion is that we do not try in any way to cut back the work of Northern Transportation Company, but rather that we take the positive approach of developing the north to such an extent that not only will Northern Transportation Company be occupied, but that the Yellowknife Company and other companies may be required to carry loads to the north and also on the return haul.
This brings up a question closely allied to the same point, in that it is time the government and the civil service looked into the question of co-operating with the provinces
Northern Transportation Company in a reassessment of Buffalo park. The Peace river changes into the Slave river just at the southern end of the park, and water transportation will be the life blood for any future development in the far north, and in Buffalo park itself.
I am sure most hon. members on all sides of the house know that our national parks have been set aside as playgrounds for future generations, and that they are not to be interfered with; but I am sure many hon. members are not aware of the situation concerning Buffalo park. However, knowing Buffalo park as I do, and as many people up there do, it is what might be called a big white elephant. We have set aside an area, approximately 14,500 square miles in my own district alone, which will never become a playground because of the distance from centres of population. It is far too large for anything like a game reserve, but it is extremely rich in minerals, gypsum and timber.
This area has never been properly explored because, as hon. members know, mineral exploration and development cannot be carried on in any Canadian national parks. This may be a quite correct policy for Banff, Jasper and other parks, but it should not apply to Buffalo park. It is time the province of Alberta and the dominion government got together and took a new look at the park. If they did, and if development took place, then Northern Transportation and any other private company that wanted to go into the north would have plenty to do. Instead of worrying about cutbacks in Fort McMurray, Waterways, Yellowknife and down the Mackenzie we would have the opportunity to provide jobs even for many of those who live in so-called southern Canada.
