During world war II uranium was an essential product which had to be manufactured for the benefit of the nation as a whole. Before the accelerated development of the Arctic both for economic and defence purposes, which began during world

Northern Transportation Company war II, which has continued ever since, and was most dynamically tackled during the six years of Conservative government, transportation was a problem that required government assistance.
The long term interests of Canada demanded that transportation routes into the north be provided, yet there was not the volume of traffic, nor even the immediate potential of traffic, needed to encourage private capital to supply transportation in the variety and quantity that was necessary. The bush pilots blazed the way in the north, but what was urgently required was road, rail and water transportation for bulk goods. In fact the development of the uranium mines in the north pointed up more than ever before the requirement for immediate acceleration of the expansion of transport for the transportation of bulk goods.
At that time the federal government, and rightly so, realized the deficiency of transportation requirements in the north and its obligations in that regard, and it assisted in the provision of those transportation facilities that did in fact open up large sections of our Arctic, and even of our sub-Arctic, during world war II. I think I need only cite the Alaska highway, and of course the establishment of Eldorado Aviation and Northern Transportation, which are both subsidiaries of Eldorado Mining and Refining Company Limited. But the true role of government, as the minister of northern affairs said so often in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories during his recent visit, was to encourage the development of private industry. With that sentiment expressed by the minister I agree wholeheartedly.
We should encourage the development of private industry, not only in mines and in farmlands, but also in the transportation field, without continuing costly government aid. This is what is happening here; because I am sure if hon. members will recall to their minds the last annual statement of Eldorado Aviation as well as that of Northern Transportation Company-but more so Eldorado Aviation-they will realize this particular operation is a submarginal one now, particularly since the cutbacks in uranium production that have appeared in recent years.
The transportation arms of both of these subsidiaries of Eldorado Mining and Refining Company Limited were set up specifically to provide transportation for the product of the government established uranium mines in the north, but instead of tax dollars being spent to provide these services, private capital should provide them as soon as the traffic flow becomes sufficient to support a privately-owned transportation network. Then, instead of money going out of the national treasury

to provide these services, money will be coming into the national treasury in the form of taxes paid by private companies operating in the Arctic.
This is not an isolated view. It is a view which is supported by Mr. Aubrey Simmons, who was the Liberal member of parliament for the Yukon until 1957, and after his defeat in 1957 became the president of Arctic Shipping Company Limited, which company of course was in direct competition with Northern Transportation Company in carrying supplies to D.E.W. line sites and things of that nature.
This whole matter was questioned in the special committee on research in 1961 when we heard evidence from Mr. Harcourt, president of Yellowknife Transportation, and Mr. Simmons of the Arctic Shipping Company Limited, and I think that Mr. Simmons made a good case. I think he was rather a good, misguided Conservative in this respect because he advocated the gradual withdrawal of Northern Transportation Company from competition with private industry in the north.
As I said before, I think the government has a proper role to play in the north where private industry is either reluctant or unable to provide investment capital to erect the framework of transportation which will meet the needs of the north and the ultimate benefit of the nation. When private industry is not willing, then the government has a responsibility to get in there and do it with the taxpayers' dollar.
Here we have a quite different situation. It was pointed up in 1961 when the special committee on research went into detail on this matter. Mr. Simmons on that occasion, when he presented the brief, had this to say.
With the growth rate in the Arctic at the present time, I submit the time has now arrived lor government to make a phased withdrawal from the field of Arctic transportation to allow private enterprise to take up a share of the burden and participate in the great adventure of development of the Arctic.
So many times in the past I have endorsed the views of Mr. Simmons, and here is yet another occasion when I am compelled to agree with my friend. Here was a man who knew the north and its requirements, and he certainly knew the inroads being made on private investment capital and private enterprise in the north by Northern Transportation Company Limited.
Mr. Simmons went on to say in the brief which he presented to the special committee on research that-
-Arctic Shipping Limited stands ready and willing to assume this responsibility. We are waiting only for the authority that must come from a responsible government source.

Mr. Simmons was not the only one who expressed these sentiments. The same sentiments were expressed by Mr. Harcourt and other officials of Yellowknife Transportation Company Limited, which is the private company operating along the Mackenzie and in the Arctic. They were also held by Mr. Harris, the vice president of Pacific Western Airlines Limited and other officials of that air line. This is not a singular problem relating to Northern Transportation Company Limited; it also involves the other subsidiary of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, namely the Eldorado Aviation Company Limited. Here is a company with a DC-4, a DC-3, and a Sikorsky 55, which they had to trade in for two other helicopters because they made a mistake in purchasing this Sikorsky. It was to be used for searching for uranium, and then the demand fell off. Here are these people, in face of a declining demand in their own operations, enlarging their own air force. It seems to me that the taxpayers' dollar is being wasted on an operation like this when there are innumerable private charter companies operating throughout the north and when there is a recognized air line company, such as Pacific Western Airlines Limited, who went on record in the special committee on research in 1961 as saying that they would provide the same service now being provided by the Eldorado Aviation Company Limited, the subsidiary of Eldorado Mining and Refining Company Limited, and at less cost per ton mile. The same guarantee was given by Yellowknife Transportation Company Limited, a company which, all credit due to it, has formed itself and grown, albeit slowly because of the competition offered by this crown corporation, Northern Transportation Company Limited, and grown in spite of a government-sponsored program to limit the development of private investment in the north.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I think the government has a responsibility in the north to provide transportation facilities when none is available from private sources. But it seems to me that when private enterprise reaches the stage where it is ready to take over and maintain services which were not there when the government entered the field, it is then time for government gradually to withdraw. I say this because it is repugnant, to my point of view, for a government openly to be competing with investment capital, particularly in the north where this capital is so important, a fact about which the minister of northern affairs left no doubt during his recent visits to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
There are several possibilities here which may meet the grievance raised by the hon.
28902-5-230
Northern Transportation Company member for Edmonton-Strathcona. One concerns the question as to what we will do with the assets of Northern Transportation Company Limited and Eldorado Aviation Limited if these companies are subject to a phased withdrawal. Again, in the committee in 1961 we had offers flatly made by the witnesses who appeared before that committee on behalf of Yellowknife Transportation and Pacific Western Airlines, that they would take over the assets of both crown companies if given half a chance. And not only that, but they went further and said by way of compromise that they would operate in conjunction with the crown-owned subsidiaries of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited. I recall quite distinctly that Pacific Western Airlines made the offer to the committee that they would be only too happy to collaborate with Yellowknife Transportation Limited ir. providing a co-ordinated water-air servict which would be not only equal to, but better than the co-ordinated service now operated by these two crown corporations.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that in order tc understand the problem it is necessary to understand the Mackenzie river transportation complex. At the time the board of transport commissioners extended their jurisdiction to the Mackenzie river system in, I believe it was, 1946 there were just four companies in the area. These companies were the Mackenzie River Transport Company, which was a division of the Hudson's Bay Company at that time and which very recently has been taken over by Northern Transportation Company Limited at the request of Mackenzie River Transport. Then there was Northern Transportation Company Limited, the company about which we are talking in this grievance raised by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. Then there was Yellowknife Transportation Limited, which operated only within the Northwest Territories. And lastly, there was Maclnnis Products Limited, which was primarily a fishing company which had a licence to transport goods within a specified area in the Mackenzie district from Fort Smith to Great Slave lake points only.
Without going in detail into the background of these four transportation companies, I think we can leave it at this, that Northern Transportation Company Limited was originally formed by Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited to service and supply their property on Great Bear lake. Eldorado was taken over by the dominion government and became a wholly-owned crown company. Northern Transportation Company Limited, in turn, became a wholly-owned subsidiary of the crown company. The original fleet of

Northern Transportation Company Northern Transportation Company Limited consisted of $140,000 worth of wooden tugs and barges. The statement recently put out by Northern Transportation indicates a rather phenomenal growth so far as these fixed assets are concerned. In 1940 Eldorado Mining and Refining shut down and Northern Transportation went into active competition as a common carrier over the entire Mackenzie river system. In 1942 Eldorado Mining and Refining reopened as a uranium producer and modern steel tugs and barges replaced the wooden vessels which had been in use. The capital expenditures of this crown company now exceed $12 million. This growth in the face of struggling private enterprise, which in the end is going to be the force which will establish efficient communication in the north, is I think beyond excuse. I would recommend to the minister of northern affairs, who I see is listening to this discussion with great interest and attention, that he very carefully consider the evidence adduced at the hearings in 1961 of the mines, forests, and waters committee. I think he will conclude, as I did, that the time for gradual government withdrawal in the field of water transportation in the Northwest Territories has arrived.
Much could be said about empire building within crown corporations. I do not intend to accuse the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company Limited of empire building because, as I have said, there was an essential service to be performed in the north in a field in which private industry either could not or would not come forward. The government acted most properly in coming to the rescue, as it should, to provide this essential service.
The time has come when we can say that Yellowknife Transportation Company can not only supply an efficient operation to provide a service equal to that now being provided by the Northern Transportation Company, but that it is capable of providing a still better service; and it seems to me to be wrong in principle that a transportation company which was established to carry ore from a mine which was set up during the war in the national interest should be allowed, after this consideration of national interest has disappeared, to expand its operation in open competition with every other water transport concern in the Arctic.
Not only that, but Northern Transportation Company is receiving preferred treatment. In all the negotiations for the D.E.W. line the only consultations which were had were carried out with Northern Transportation Company. No bids were called from private enterprise. The United States government said it needed to move so many millions of tons of material to the D.E.W. line stations. It inquired what carriers were operating and


was informed that the carrier was Northern Transportation Company. Nothing was said about other carriers in the area and the result was that the whole of the operation was given to Northern Transportation. It seems to me wrong in principle that such a state of affairs should be allowed to exist. I believe the government would save money by calling for open tenders. I recall very well, in the evidence given in 1961, the operators of the private transportation company saying they could compete and transport the freight at a price less than that being charged by Northern Transportation Company.
I found it surprising that in the face of this evidence the Minister of Trade and Commerce could say the other day that the operations of the company in the north would be not only continued, but expanded, at a time when we have a struggling company in the north which is trying to provide a service supported by private investment capital. This is an instance of the government eroding the foundations of something which the minister himself in his visits to the north praised so highly and declared we should encourage, namely the development of private capital investment. I think the government should take a hard second look at the need for the continued existence of Northern Transportation Company and of Eldorado Aviation. The latter concern is in an even worse position than is Northern Transportation in this regard, because there is a vibrant air industry in the north backed up by years of growth from the days of bush pilots to the present time. The circumstances here are different from those which apply to water transport.
I am glad to see the minister of northern affairs (Mr. Laing) in his place tonight during discussion of this grievance. I urge him to take a hard look at the minutes of the special committee on research in 1961 and do all he can to convince his hard-shelled colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), to have a change of heart. I know that the real interests of the minister are in the north. At least, if he is to remain where he is he has to convey that impression. This is one area more than in any other in which the hon. gentleman can reassure northerners of the sincerity of his belief in the principle he so often enunciated during his visit to the north last summer, namely that the northern part of this country must attract investment capital. This will not be done unless government gets out of fields which private investment capital is ready, willing and able to enter. One of these fields is transportation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext:
It is my good fortune to be in the house tonight at a time when the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not here because, had he been present, he would no doubt have made a reply to the objections raised by hon. members with respect to the type of transportation provided in the Northwest Territories.
I think this has been a good debate. We are dealing here with the lifeline of the Northwest Territories. In a pioneer country-and this is a pioneer country-transportation comes first, and we are dealing in this instance with the jugular vein of transportation in the territories, namely transportation along the Mackenzie river. I think there is a certain principle to be adopted with respect to the use of public moneys as against private moneys, and I think this principle is held by my own party as well as by the party of the hon. members who have spoken here tonight. I would like to think that public money will be used only to provide a necessary service when private money is either unable or unwilling to provide that service. In such cases it is justifiable to make the required service available out of public money.
I believe the history of the company under discussion will show that it was built up to serve a need which was not met by private enterprise. Now the situation is changing, and the population is growing. However, the Northwest Territories is still a deficit area. They are a very heavy deficit area. I think the people of Canada should know that for every dollar the Northwest Territories are providing in revenue today, other parts of Canada are providing $12. That is a situation we want to reverse. It is one we do not like and we have to make certain definite plans for the future that will overcome it.
28902-5-2304
Northern Transportation Company
I think that the first requirement in a pioneer country is to have reasonable transportation. If it cannot be supplied by private capital then it will have to be supplied by public capital. I think there is an element of subsidization. Certainly there is an advance of funds in respect of the railway now being built from Grimshaw to Hay River and Pine Point. I am going to suggest to the house that in a very few years it will be one of the most advantageous railways in Canada because it is serving the Mackenzie and also serving the great Pine Point mine.
The private companies that have grown up there are rendering excellent service. I think they are expanding. I saw the other day that the private company proposes to put on a vessel to take tourist passengers down the Mackenzie. I predict it will be booked full from the first day it operates because there could be no more interesting holiday trip than a return trip on the Mackenzie river. The equipment of the private company is improving all the time. The service to the customers is better. I believe there have been some reductions in rates, although they have not been large, and this is a high rate area for a variety of causes.
In the Northwest Territories we want to develop as many mines, as many oil wells, as many industries as we possibly can so that the territories will become self-sufficient. We want to try to bring the costs of doing business in the Northwest Territories and also in the Yukon territory as close as we possibly can to the costs of doing business and the cost of labour and everything else in the area of southern Canada. Otherwise the mining properties and other properties in the north would be highgraded, only the best would be taken out, and when we finally came to develop the country it would seem to me we would have to develop it on a general subsidization plan. But if we can bring the cost of doing business in the Northwest Territories approximately to the level of that in southern Canada we will develop the country as it properly should be.
I think we are making very good progress in recent years. As I said before, the Northwest Territories are a deficit area. The people who live there should not be ashamed of that. When the Northwest Territories were fronting not many years ago the luxuriant provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan of today, there were not very many dollars around in those days in the region that now comprises Alberta and Saskatchewan. So we should not be ashamed of putting social capital into this region. I am quite certain we will retrieve that social capital only by encouraging private investment capital to go in there. We can do so in no other way. Otherwise

Northern Transportation Company we shall have a permanent situation of putting funds in there, and that is something which the taxpayers of southern Canada do not want any more than the people who live in the Northwest Territories.
In my view it is a question of balancing *out our situation at the present time. What all transportation companies require, it seems to me, is the same thing that the head of an American railroad once said railways require. He said that they require to see to it that the longest possible distance exists between the locomotive and the caboose. I think that applies to every transportation company. What we need to do is not to divide the pie between the private company and the public company but rather to increase the size of the pie.
I was in the Northwest Territories not long ago and visited Hay River. I am quite certain that hon. members who have spoken tonight will confirm that they have had a very good year on the Mackenzie river. In spite of the terrific damage to Hay River early in May, shipping out of Hay River up the Mackenzie has increased by 50 per cent over last year. The two companies, one private and the other public, have shared the business fairly well and the fact that they are in competition has probably had the effect of keeping costs down somewhat to some of the consumers.
I am sure the house would not want to see a wholly owned public or national company without private competition. I know that the people to whom shipments are made up there would not want to see that situation, and at this particular juncture the fact that Northern Transportation is operating there with public funds probably has an effect upon the rates charged by the private company.
I am concerned that the private company does not lose money, and I do not think they are losing money. With the increase in the amount of shipping on that great river, which I predict is going to be phenomenal in the next few years, I think that the private company will have the opportunity of making headway, and as a policy I would suggest that as time goes on those of us who believe in incentive and the prize should do our very best to encourage the investment of increasing amounts of private capital in the Northwest Territories. That is what I want. I think that is a prerequisite to the health and welfare of that area.
This can apply to those particular investments and activities in which the national government now takes a part. In other words, I think that as quickly as is in the public interest we should move toward a policy

that will increase private investment in that area. In my view the debate tonight has been productive of considerable good. As the minister responsible for the Northwest Territories and for the Yukon I, of course, like to see them discussed in the House of Commons.
I do say to hon. members that in the immediate years ahead, particularly on the western side of the north, spectacular and very great things are going to happen. We have problems. Social capital has to be put in there. The sooner we can retrieve it the better for all of us and it can be retrieved only by private risk capital being invested in that region.

speechtext: Would the minister permit one question? In view of his sentiments concerning the encouragement of private investment capital in the north, sentiments with which I agree 100 per cent, will he undertake to consult with his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), with a view to calling for tenders for government freight, including D.E.W. line freight which is not now going to public tender, in order to obtain competitive bids on the part of the private operator along the Mackenzie and the government supported operation, Northern Transportation Company? If the government did that I believe they would find that the competition would bring about a lowering in the per ton rates along the Mackenzie basin, and along the Arctic coast as well.
